title: Yara and the Winter
premise: Lena Eriksen, a meticulous pest controller, is called to the isolated Yarrow farmhouse where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. She documents everything—photos, logs, and overnight sleep recordings of the family—because documentation is a kind of prayer against disbelief. But the recordings capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, and Lena realizes the entity has been counting the household, and that her own presence has added a name to its ledger. To save the family she must break her own rules of invisibility, confront what the house inherited from the family's dead patriarch, and get them out before the count completes—even though leaving means admitting the thing will simply follow the bloodline.
about_author: Edmund Yarrow is the pen name of a former building inspector from rural Minnesota who spent a decade documenting structural decay in abandoned farmhouses. He writes horror about paperwork, isolation, and the terrible arithmetic of families.

chapters.title: The Call Sheet
chapters.summary: Lena Eriksen takes a routine pest control job at the remote Yarrow farm after three prior contractors quit. POV: Lena. She notices fingerprints on the inside of sealed upstairs windows—small, adult-sized, pressed hard enough to warp the glass. Emotional beat: professional unease disguised as competence; she starts a log because that's what she does.

chapters.title: Household of Four
chapters.summary: Lena meets the family: exhausted mother Ingrid, sullen teenage son Anders, quiet daughter Maja, and grandmother Halvor's empty room, kept exactly as he left it. POV: Lena. The mother insists the problem is mice. Emotional beat: the wrongness of a house where one room is a shrine and everyone speaks in lowered voices.

chapters.title: What the Traps Catch
chapters.summary: Lena sets traps and dusts for tracks; by morning every trap is sprung, empty, and arranged in a neat line on the kitchen table. POV: Lena. No footprints in the dust she laid. Emotional beat: her documentation instinct kicks into overdrive—she photographs everything, telling herself it's for the report.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Lab results on lifted prints come back inconclusive: human ridge patterns, but pressure depth impossible for a living hand. POV: Lena, with a phone call to a skeptical former colleague. Emotional beat: the first crack in her rational armor; she rereads her own notes and finds entries she doesn't remember writing.

chapters.title: The Recorder
chapters.summary: Lena installs audio recorders in the bedrooms, framing it as standard monitoring for nocturnal activity. POV: Lena. Ingrid almost refuses, then agrees too quickly, as if she'd been waiting for someone to listen. Emotional beat: complicity—the family knows more than they're saying, and Lena lets herself be hired anyway.

chapters.title: First Night Recording
chapters.summary: The recording captures eight hours of breathing, sleep-talking—and at 3:11 a.m., a second voice, dry and patient, answering questions nobody asked. POV: Lena alone in her truck at dawn. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into purpose; she plays it four times and transcribes it word for word, hands shaking.

chapters.title: Transcription
chapters.summary: The voice asks the sleeping family questions: names, dates, who remembers whom. It repeats Halvor's name like it's checking an inventory. POV: alternating Lena and Maja, who has heard the voice for years and thought everyone did. Emotional beat: Maja's relief at being believed collides with Lena's guilt at what listening has cost the child.

chapters.title: Ingrid's Confession
chapters.summary: Ingrid admits Halvor made a bargain decades ago—prosperity in exchange for being remembered, precisely and forever. The thing in the house is the memory itself, keeping count. POV: Ingrid, finally. Emotional beat: shame and defiance braided together; she stayed because leaving felt like betraying the dead man's sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Lena searches Halvor's room and finds his own documentation: sixty years of ledgers listing every family member, every visitor, every name spoken in the house—including, dated last week, hers. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: the hunter discovering she is on the list; invisibility was never an option once she signed the work order.

chapters.title: Anders Runs
chapters.summary: Terrified by Lena's questions, Anders flees to a friend's house ten miles away. That night the recordings catch the second voice in HIS room there, patient, asking its questions. POV: Anders. Emotional beat: the horrifying confirmation that distance means nothing—the count follows the blood, not the walls.

chapters.title: Rules of the Count
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing Halvor's ledgers with parish records, Lena deduces the pattern: the entity finishes a count when every named member has answered its questions aloud in sleep. Three of five have already answered. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: cold clarity—she now knows the deadline but not how to beat it, and telling the family may hasten it.

chapters.title: Maja's Answers
chapters.summary: Lena reviews old tapes and realizes Maja has been answering the voice since age six—fluent, unafraid, almost fond. POV: Maja. She reveals the voice showed her Halvor's memories, taught her the farm's history no one else remembered. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth—Maja loves the thing that is counting her, and begs Lena not to take it away.

chapters.title: Cutting the Line
chapters.summary: Lena proposes erasing the family from the ledger: legally dissolving the estate, changing names, severing inheritance. Ingrid resists—Halvor built everything, and surrendering the land feels like letting him be forgotten twice. POV: Ingrid. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh; survival priced against memory, and a mother choosing which debt to default on.

chapters.title: The Lawyer in the Town
chapters.summary: A trip to town to file the estate dissolution goes wrong: the county clerk's records for the Yarrow parcel are blank, then wrong, then written in handwriting that matches Halvor's ledgers. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: institutional gaslighting—the bureaucracy itself seems to have been edited, and Lena's own work order has vanished from her company's system.

chapters.title: What Lena Forgot
chapters.summary: Lena discovers a recording of herself asleep in the guest room, answering the voice—her mother's maiden name, her childhood street, things she never told anyone here. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: violation and vertigo; the documenter has been documented, and her careful logbook now contains pages in her own hand describing events she cannot recall.

chapters.title: The Last Room
chapters.summary: Following the voice's questions backward, Lena opens a bricked pantry behind Halvor's room and finds the original bargain's evidence: Halvor didn't summon the entity—he inherited it, same as the house, same as the debt, going back past the first Yarrow. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as predation; the family fortune was always a lure to keep the bloodline close and countable.

chapters.title: Bargaining with the Voice
chapters.summary: Lena stays awake all night and speaks to the entity directly, offering herself as a completed entry if it releases the others. The voice considers, then counters: it doesn't want her—it wants to be REMEMBERED, and only a living heir can carry it out of the house. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: the horror of realizing the trap's true shape—the count was never to keep them in, but to choose who carries it out.

chapters.title: Maja's Choice
chapters.summary: Maja volunteers; the voice has been her teacher, her companion, the only one who never lied to her. POV: Maja and Lena in brutal negotiation. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth inverted—a child's love for the monster versus an outsider's duty to save her; Lena must decide whether saving Maja means taking away the only thing that ever listened to her.

chapters.title: The Night of the Count
chapters.summary: The final count begins early: doors open and close on their own, every clock reads 3:11, and the voice moves room to room completing its inventory. Lena burns Halvor's ledgers page by page while Ingrid gets the children to the trucks. POV: rotating through all four. Emotional beat: climax—chaos, sacrifice, and the terrible discovery that burning the ledger adds fuel, because fire is also a memory.

chapters.title: Out Ahead of It
chapters.summary: They escape as the farmhouse lights die behind them, Lena having offered the voice a compromise: she will document IT—write its history, publish it, remember it publicly—so it no longer needs a bloodline to be remembered. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: hollow victory; the entity accepts, the family drives through snow toward daylight, and Lena understands she has just become its new keeper.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Weeks later: Ingrid and the kids are in an apartment in Duluth, adjusting, sleeping soundly—for now. Anders won't speak of it; Maja writes letters to the voice and burns them. POV: Ingrid. Emotional beat: fragile recovery shadowed by doubt—they were saved, but nothing was destroyed, only renegotiated.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Lena finishes her report, then begins the book she promised the voice—a manuscript titled 'Yarrow and the Winter.' On the last page, in handwriting not quite her own, a new entry appears: a name, a date next month, a family in another town. POV: Lena. Emotional beat: chilling resolution—the price of survival was becoming the instrument of the next count, and the prayer of documentation was always addressed to something that answers.
